## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.

## How the AKC compiles its annual breed popularity rankings
Credit: Helena Lopes / Pexels
The AKC builds its popularity list entirely from registration paperwork, counting how many dogs of each recognized breed were enrolled with the club during the prior calendar year. No survey, poll or public vote feeds into it. The club publishes the ranked results the following year, leading with the top five and listing the full standings beneath.
That methodology shapes what the list can and cannot tell you. Founded in 1884, the AKC operates as a purebred registry and recognizes roughly 200 breeds across seven groups — sporting, hound, working, terrier, toy, non-sporting and herding — plus a miscellaneous class for breeds working toward full recognition. Registration is voluntary and carries a fee, and the owners most likely to pay it are breeders documenting litters and handlers preparing to compete in conformation, agility or obedience.
The ranking therefore measures purebred registration activity, not total dog ownership. Mixed-breed dogs never appear in the breed standings, though the AKC enrolls them separately through its Canine Partners program so they can compete in club sports. A breed can be common in American households and still rank modestly if its owners skip the paperwork, while breeds with active show and performance communities register at rates well above their share of the pet population.
The archive is what makes the data useful. The AKC keeps year-by-year rankings going back more than a decade, which is how long-term shifts become visible rather than anecdotal. Because registrations are tallied after the year closes, each list describes a year already finished rather than current demand. Single-year movement among breeds ranked in the 40s or 80s can come down to a handful of litters, so the trend line carries more weight than any one year's position.
Read as a gauge of registered purebred demand, the list is reliable. Read as a count of every dog living in the U.S., it is incomplete by design.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +2.00% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.
texts.7:
## How the AKC compiles its annual breed popularity rankings
Credit: Helena Lopes / Pexels
The AKC builds its popularity list entirely from registration paperwork, counting how many dogs of each recognized breed were enrolled with the club during the prior calendar year. No survey, poll or public vote feeds into it. The club publishes the ranked results the following year, leading with the top five and listing the full standings beneath.
That methodology shapes what the list can and cannot tell you. Founded in 1884, the AKC operates as a purebred registry and recognizes roughly 200 breeds across seven groups — sporting, hound, working, terrier, toy, non-sporting and herding — plus a miscellaneous class for breeds working toward full recognition. Registration is voluntary and carries a fee, and the owners most likely to pay it are breeders documenting litters and handlers preparing to compete in conformation, agility or obedience.
The ranking therefore measures purebred registration activity, not total dog ownership. Mixed-breed dogs never appear in the breed standings, though the AKC enrolls them separately through its Canine Partners program so they can compete in club sports. A breed can be common in American households and still rank modestly if its owners skip the paperwork, while breeds with active show and performance communities register at rates well above their share of the pet population.
The archive is what makes the data useful. The AKC keeps year-by-year rankings going back more than a decade, which is how long-term shifts become visible rather than anecdotal. Because registrations are tallied after the year closes, each list describes a year already finished rather than current demand. Single-year movement among breeds ranked in the 40s or 80s can come down to a handful of litters, so the trend line carries more weight than any one year's position.
Read as a gauge of registered purebred demand, the list is reliable. Read as a count of every dog living in the U.S., it is incomplete by design.
texts.8:
## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +2.00% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.
texts.9:
## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.

## How the AKC compiles its annual breed popularity rankings
Credit: Helena Lopes / Pexels
The AKC builds its popularity list entirely from registration paperwork, counting how many dogs of each recognized breed were enrolled with the club during the prior calendar year. No survey, poll or public vote feeds into it. The club publishes the ranked results the following year, leading with the top five and listing the full standings beneath.
That methodology shapes what the list can and cannot tell you. Founded in 1884, the AKC operates as a purebred registry and recognizes roughly 200 breeds across seven groups — sporting, hound, working, terrier, toy, non-sporting and herding — plus a miscellaneous class for breeds working toward full recognition. Registration is voluntary and carries a fee, and the owners most likely to pay it are breeders documenting litters and handlers preparing to compete in conformation, agility or obedience.
The ranking therefore measures purebred registration activity, not total dog ownership. Mixed-breed dogs never appear in the breed standings, though the AKC enrolls them separately through its Canine Partners program so they can compete in club sports. A breed can be common in American households and still rank modestly if its owners skip the paperwork, while breeds with active show and performance communities register at rates well above their share of the pet population.
The archive is what makes the data useful. The AKC keeps year-by-year rankings going back more than a decade, which is how long-term shifts become visible rather than anecdotal. Because registrations are tallied after the year closes, each list describes a year already finished rather than current demand. Single-year movement among breeds ranked in the 40s or 80s can come down to a handful of litters, so the trend line carries more weight than any one year's position.
Read as a gauge of registered purebred demand, the list is reliable. Read as a count of every dog living in the U.S., it is incomplete by design.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +2.00% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
By Melanie Haid
Updated: Aug 11, 2026 | 5 Minutes
Updated: Aug 11, 2026 | 5 Minutes
*   labrador retriever  
*   french bulldog  
*   most popular breeds
As the world’s largest registry of purebred dogs, the AKC uses our registration statistics to rank the most popular breeds of the past year — and the numbers are in!
The French Bulldog has secured the No. 1 spot as the most popular dog breed in the United States for the third year in a row. In 2022, the Frenchie took the Most Popular title from the Labrador Retriever, a breed who had previously sat comfortably at No. 1 for 31 years.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Staying in the No.1 Spot
French Bulldogs have surged to the top, quickly amassing popularity for their size and adaptability. It’s hard to miss their signature bat ears on city streets and rural roads alike.
Over the last 12 years, they’ve climbed the rankings. In 2012, they were ranked the No. 14 most popular breed, and by 2021, they’d made it to the No. 2 spot. They officially became the No.1 breed in 2022, and have held that title for three years now.
French Bulldogs are especially popular in cities, but their playful nature and compact size are great for a variety of lifestyles. These little dogs originated in France, and French Bulldog history is complex. They were recognized by the American Kennel Club in 1898, and now have over 100 years of AKC history behind them.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Top 10 Dog Breeds of 2024
The top five and top 10 dog breeds are popular for a reason, and typically don’t shift too much. The Frenchie is again at No. 1, followed by the Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever, German Shepherd Dog, and Poodle at No. 5.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
2024 saw major shifts for a lot of breeds across the rankings. While some breeds surged over 20 rankings higher, others shifted 10 or more rankings lower. Many breeds, especially in the 20s and 30s, stayed at the same spot from 2023 to 2024.
The Danish-Swedish Farmdog, which debuted in January 2025 as part of the Working Group as the 202nd AKC-recognized breed will be included in the registration rankings for 2025. The Lancashire Heeler, which became AKC-recognized in January 2024, debuted in the 2024 rankings at No. 189.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
### Climbing the Rankings
The biggest surges in popularity among breeds came from four very different dog breeds. The Kerry Blue Terrier had the highest jump, moving up a whopping 25 spots from No. 160 to No. 135. The Bracco Italiano, recognized by the AKC in 2022, continues to move up. From 2023 to 2024, the Bracco moved up 20 spots from No. 152 to No. 132.

The Brussels Griffon, American Eskimo Dog, and Harrier all went up 13 placements. The Brussels Griffon moved from No. 92 to No. 84, the Eskie from No. 129 to No. 116, and the Harrier from No. 190 to No. 183.
The Mudi, recognized in 2022, continues to climb the ranks, going up 12 from No. 130 in 2023 to No. 122 in 2024. The Polish Lowland Sheepdog also went up 12 spots, from No. 193 to No. 181.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
### Climbing the Rankings
The Manchester Terrier went up 11 ranks from No. 126 to No. 115, and the Boykin Spaniel went up 10 rankings from No. 75 to No. 65.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
### Moving Down on the List

The Black and Tan Coonhound went down 20 spots, from No. 131 to No. 151. Down 17 from 2023 to 2024, the Wirehaired Vizsla went from the No. 142 spot to No. 159.

The Chinese Shar-Pei went from No. 70 to No. 83, down 13 spots. Also down 13 spots was the Field Spaniel, from No. 147 to No. 160.
Each down 12 spots were the Bergamasco Sheepdog, the Old English Sheepdog, and the Dogue de Bordeaux. They went from No. 188 to No. 200, No. 77 to No. 89, and No. 84 to No. 96 respectfully.
Other big dogs have moved down as well. The Neapolitan Mastiff and Great Pyrenees are both down 10 spots. The Neapolitan Mastiff went from No. 118 to No. 128, and the Pyr went from No. 64 to No. 74.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
### Holding Their Spots
These breeds found solace in their 2023 placements and stayed there. The top five breeds stayed the same, but so did the Shih Tzu at No. 20, Pomeranian at No. 22, Boston Terrier at No. 23, and Havanese at No. 25. In the 30s, Belgian Malinois stayed at No. 33, Basset Hounds stayed at No. 34, Vizsla stayed at No. 35, and the Maltese stayed at No. 37. The German Wirehaired Pointer stayed at No. 61, and the Chow Chow stayed at No. 88. The Finnish Spitz kept their spot at No. 194.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Least Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
Often rare breeds, the dogs in the bottom 20 have the lowest numbers in terms of registration in the United States. There are 201 breeds counted since the addition of the Lancashire Heeler in 2024, and there will be 202 for 2025 when the registration numbers for the Danish-Swedish Farmdog are added.
The Sloughi, which was ranked last at No. 200 in 2023, has made the jump to No. 197 in 2024. They’re followed by the Norwegian Lundehund at No. 198, the Grand Basset Griffon Vendeen at No. 199, the Bergamasco Sheepdog at No. 200, and the English Foxhound at No. 201. The English Foxhound was ranked 199 in 2023, and dropped two spots in 2024.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
By Melanie Haid
Updated: Aug 11, 2026 | 5 Minutes
Updated: Aug 11, 2026 | 5 Minutes
*   labrador retriever  
*   french bulldog  
*   most popular breeds
As the world’s largest registry of purebred dogs, the AKC uses our registration statistics to rank the most popular breeds of the past year — and the numbers are in!
The French Bulldog has secured the No. 1 spot as the most popular dog breed in the United States for the third year in a row. In 2022, the Frenchie took the Most Popular title from the Labrador Retriever, a breed who had previously sat comfortably at No. 1 for 31 years.
texts.69:
# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Staying in the No.1 Spot
French Bulldogs have surged to the top, quickly amassing popularity for their size and adaptability. It’s hard to miss their signature bat ears on city streets and rural roads alike.
Over the last 12 years, they’ve climbed the rankings. In 2012, they were ranked the No. 14 most popular breed, and by 2021, they’d made it to the No. 2 spot. They officially became the No.1 breed in 2022, and have held that title for three years now.
French Bulldogs are especially popular in cities, but their playful nature and compact size are great for a variety of lifestyles. These little dogs originated in France, and French Bulldog history is complex. They were recognized by the American Kennel Club in 1898, and now have over 100 years of AKC history behind them.

The top five and top 10 dog breeds are popular for a reason, and typically don’t shift too much. The Frenchie is again at No. 1, followed by the Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever, German Shepherd Dog, and Poodle at No. 5.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
2024 saw major shifts for a lot of breeds across the rankings. While some breeds surged over 20 rankings higher, others shifted 10 or more rankings lower. Many breeds, especially in the 20s and 30s, stayed at the same spot from 2023 to 2024.
The Danish-Swedish Farmdog, which debuted in January 2025 as part of the Working Group as the 202nd AKC-recognized breed will be included in the registration rankings for 2025. The Lancashire Heeler, which became AKC-recognized in January 2024, debuted in the 2024 rankings at No. 189.

### Climbing the Rankings
The biggest surges in popularity among breeds came from four very different dog breeds. The Kerry Blue Terrier had the highest jump, moving up a whopping 25 spots from No. 160 to No. 135. The Bracco Italiano, recognized by the AKC in 2022, continues to move up. From 2023 to 2024, the Bracco moved up 20 spots from No. 152 to No. 132.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
By Melanie Haid
Updated: Aug 11, 2026 | 5 Minutes

As the world’s largest registry of purebred dogs, the AKC uses our registration statistics to rank the most popular breeds of the past year — and the numbers are in!
The French Bulldog has secured the No. 1 spot as the most popular dog breed in the United States for the third year in a row. In 2022, the Frenchie took the Most Popular title from the Labrador Retriever, a breed who had previously sat comfortably at No. 1 for 31 years.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Staying in the No.1 Spot
French Bulldogs have surged to the top, quickly amassing popularity for their size and adaptability. It’s hard to miss their signature bat ears on city streets and rural roads alike.
Over the last 12 years, they’ve climbed the rankings. In 2012, they were ranked the No. 14 most popular breed, and by 2021, they’d made it to the No. 2 spot. They officially became the No.1 breed in 2022, and have held that title for three years now.
French Bulldogs are especially popular in cities, but their playful nature and compact size are great for a variety of lifestyles. These little dogs originated in France, and French Bulldog history is complex. They were recognized by the American Kennel Club in 1898, and now have over 100 years of AKC history behind them.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Top 10 Dog Breeds of 2024
The top five and top 10 dog breeds are popular for a reason, and typically don’t shift too much. The Frenchie is again at No. 1, followed by the Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever, German Shepherd Dog, and Poodle at No. 5.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2024
## Big Shifts of Note in 2024
2024 saw major shifts for a lot of breeds across the rankings. While some breeds surged over 20 rankings higher, others shifted 10 or more rankings lower. Many breeds, especially in the 20s and 30s, stayed at the same spot from 2023 to 2024.
The Danish-Swedish Farmdog, which debuted in January 2025 as part of the Working Group as the 202nd AKC-recognized breed will be included in the registration rankings for 2025. The Lancashire Heeler, which became AKC-recognized in January 2024, debuted in the 2024 rankings at No. 189.

## The Top 10 Most Popular Dog Breeds in America in 2017
Today, the American Kennel Club announced the results of their annual survey of the most popular dog breeds in America, and once again, the **Labrador Retriever** took the top spot. For 27 years in a row, the Lab has been #1 on the list, which is determined by the AKC based on the number of registrations received. Title: The 5 most popular dog breeds in America, per the AKC

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.

## How the AKC compiles its annual breed popularity rankings
Credit: Helena Lopes / Pexels
The AKC builds its popularity list entirely from registration paperwork, counting how many dogs of each recognized breed were enrolled with the club during the prior calendar year. No survey, poll or public vote feeds into it. The club publishes the ranked results the following year, leading with the top five and listing the full standings beneath.
That methodology shapes what the list can and cannot tell you. Founded in 1884, the AKC operates as a purebred registry and recognizes roughly 200 breeds across seven groups — sporting, hound, working, terrier, toy, non-sporting and herding — plus a miscellaneous class for breeds working toward full recognition. Registration is voluntary and carries a fee, and the owners most likely to pay it are breeders documenting litters and handlers preparing to compete in conformation, agility or obedience.
The ranking therefore measures purebred registration activity, not total dog ownership. Mixed-breed dogs never appear in the breed standings, though the AKC enrolls them separately through its Canine Partners program so they can compete in club sports. A breed can be common in American households and still rank modestly if its owners skip the paperwork, while breeds with active show and performance communities register at rates well above their share of the pet population.
The archive is what makes the data useful. The AKC keeps year-by-year rankings going back more than a decade, which is how long-term shifts become visible rather than anecdotal. Because registrations are tallied after the year closes, each list describes a year already finished rather than current demand. Single-year movement among breeds ranked in the 40s or 80s can come down to a handful of litters, so the trend line carries more weight than any one year's position.
Read as a gauge of registered purebred demand, the list is reliable. Read as a count of every dog living in the U.S., it is incomplete by design.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +2.00% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.

## How the AKC compiles its annual breed popularity rankings
Credit: Helena Lopes / Pexels
The AKC builds its popularity list entirely from registration paperwork, counting how many dogs of each recognized breed were enrolled with the club during the prior calendar year. No survey, poll or public vote feeds into it. The club publishes the ranked results the following year, leading with the top five and listing the full standings beneath.
That methodology shapes what the list can and cannot tell you. Founded in 1884, the AKC operates as a purebred registry and recognizes roughly 200 breeds across seven groups — sporting, hound, working, terrier, toy, non-sporting and herding — plus a miscellaneous class for breeds working toward full recognition. Registration is voluntary and carries a fee, and the owners most likely to pay it are breeders documenting litters and handlers preparing to compete in conformation, agility or obedience.
The ranking therefore measures purebred registration activity, not total dog ownership. Mixed-breed dogs never appear in the breed standings, though the AKC enrolls them separately through its Canine Partners program so they can compete in club sports. A breed can be common in American households and still rank modestly if its owners skip the paperwork, while breeds with active show and performance communities register at rates well above their share of the pet population.
The archive is what makes the data useful. The AKC keeps year-by-year rankings going back more than a decade, which is how long-term shifts become visible rather than anecdotal. Because registrations are tallied after the year closes, each list describes a year already finished rather than current demand. Single-year movement among breeds ranked in the 40s or 80s can come down to a handful of litters, so the trend line carries more weight than any one year's position.
Read as a gauge of registered purebred demand, the list is reliable. Read as a count of every dog living in the U.S., it is incomplete by design.
texts.8:
## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +2.00% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.
texts.9:
## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.

## How the AKC compiles its annual breed popularity rankings
Credit: Helena Lopes / Pexels
The AKC builds its popularity list entirely from registration paperwork, counting how many dogs of each recognized breed were enrolled with the club during the prior calendar year. No survey, poll or public vote feeds into it. The club publishes the ranked results the following year, leading with the top five and listing the full standings beneath.
That methodology shapes what the list can and cannot tell you. Founded in 1884, the AKC operates as a purebred registry and recognizes roughly 200 breeds across seven groups — sporting, hound, working, terrier, toy, non-sporting and herding — plus a miscellaneous class for breeds working toward full recognition. Registration is voluntary and carries a fee, and the owners most likely to pay it are breeders documenting litters and handlers preparing to compete in conformation, agility or obedience.
The ranking therefore measures purebred registration activity, not total dog ownership. Mixed-breed dogs never appear in the breed standings, though the AKC enrolls them separately through its Canine Partners program so they can compete in club sports. A breed can be common in American households and still rank modestly if its owners skip the paperwork, while breeds with active show and performance communities register at rates well above their share of the pet population.
The archive is what makes the data useful. The AKC keeps year-by-year rankings going back more than a decade, which is how long-term shifts become visible rather than anecdotal. Because registrations are tallied after the year closes, each list describes a year already finished rather than current demand. Single-year movement among breeds ranked in the 40s or 80s can come down to a handful of litters, so the trend line carries more weight than any one year's position.
Read as a gauge of registered purebred demand, the list is reliable. Read as a count of every dog living in the U.S., it is incomplete by design.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +2.00% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.
